questions.title: Cable angle and lifting power
questions.subtopic: Cable angle and lifting power
questions.stem: A load is raised vertically at constant speed by two symmetrical cables, each at angle $\theta$ to the vertical. What are the ratios of the new tension in one cable to its original tension, and of the new useful lifting power to its original value?

sourceAnchors.focus: Resolved tension and rate of gravitational-energy transfer

questions.title: Where an impact removes most rotation
questions.subtopic: Where an impact removes most rotation
questions.stem: A horizontal turntable has moment of inertia $I$ and initial angular speed $\omega$. Clay of mass $m$ is dropped vertically and sticks at radius $r$, with $mr^2=I$. In a separate identical trial it sticks at radius $r/2$. External torque about the axis is negligible. What is the ratio of rotational kinetic energy lost in the first trial to that lost in the second?

sourceAnchors.focus: Off-axis sticking collision and rotational-energy loss

questions.changeNotes: Uses two impact radii and a nonlinear energy-loss ratio rather than identifying a graph.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Combine angular-momentum conservation with dissipated rotational energy.

verification.method: Reproducible author calculation, dimensional and limiting-case checks
verification.notes: Physical reasoning and distractor uniqueness: Conservation of angular momentum gives $\omega_f=I\omega/(I+mr^2)$ and $\Delta K/K_i=mr^2/(I+mr^2)$. The losses are $K_i/2$ and $K_i/5$, respectively. Their ratio is $5/2$, not $4$: the final angular speed also changes with radius.; Ratio of rotational losses = 2.5

questions.title: A rolling cylinder at a later time
questions.subtopic: A rolling cylinder at a later time
questions.stem: A uniform solid cylinder rolls without slipping from rest down a straight incline. Its moment of inertia is $I=\tfrac12MR^2$. When its angular momentum about its centre has doubled, what is the factor by which its vertical drop has increased, and what fraction of its total kinetic energy is translational? The incline and $g$ are constant.

questions.title: Radiation into warm surroundings
questions.subtopic: Radiation into warm surroundings
questions.stem: A black surface of area $A$ at temperature $T$ radiates into surroundings at negligible temperature, with net power $P$. A second surface has area $2A$, temperature $2T$ and emissivity $0.25$. It is surrounded by a large enclosure at temperature $T$. What is its net outward radiative power? Assume absorptivity equals emissivity.

sourceAnchors.focus: Area, emissivity and fourth-power radiative scaling

questions.changeNotes: Adds finite-temperature surroundings and asks for net rather than emitted power.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Distinguish emission from net energy transfer before scaling.

verification.method: Reproducible author calculation, dimensional and limiting-case checks

The $8P$ distractor neglects absorbed enclosure radiation; using the temperature difference to the fourth power is also incorrect.; Net-radiation factor = 7.5

questions.title: A measured thermal-contact discontinuity
questions.subtopic: A measured thermal-contact discontinuity
questions.stem: Two identical bars conduct heat steadily between reservoirs at $100^\circ\mathrm C$ and $0^\circ\mathrm C$. Each bar has thermal resistance $R$. An imperfect contact separates them: its hot-side and cold-side temperatures are measured as $60^\circ\mathrm C$ and $40^\circ\mathrm C$. For any element, a supplied model is $\Delta T=\dot Q R_{\rm th}$, where $\dot Q$ is the heat-transfer rate. The contact resistance is then doubled while bar resistances and reservoir temperatures stay fixed. What are the new-to-old heat-rate ratio and the new hot-side contact temperature?

sourceAnchors.focus: Steady conduction through joined bars

questions.changeNotes: Replaces a bare two-conductivity calculation by inferring an unknown interface resistance from a temperature discontinuity, then changing that contact.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Interpret a new supplied resistance model and recompute the entire temperature distribution after a controlled contact change.

verification.method: Reproducible author calculation, dimensional and limiting-case checks
verification.notes: Physical reasoning and distractor uniqueness: Initially each bar has a $40\,\mathrm K$ drop, while the contact has $20\,\mathrm K$, so its resistance is $R/2$. The old contact temperatures do not remain fixed.; Inferred contact/bar resistance ratio = 0.5 ; Changed heat-transfer ratio = 0.8333333333 ; Changed hot-side contact temperature = 66.66666667 deg C

questions.title: Testing a closest-approach model
questions.subtopic: Testing a closest-approach model
questions.stem:
A research-training simulation produces synthetic data for head-on alpha scattering from heavy stationary nuclei. Outside the nucleus, the purely electrostatic model predicts $d=K/E$ and $K=2Z(1.44\,\mathrm{MeV\,fm})$, where $E$ is incident alpha kinetic energy, $d$ is closest approach, and $Z$ is target proton number. Binding and target recoil are neglected. Each $d$ has uncertainty $\pm0.5\,\mathrm{fm}$; energy uncertainty is negligible. The reciprocal-energy graph represents these data.

| $E/\mathrm{MeV}$ | 3.00 | 4.00 | 5.00 | 6.00 | 8.00 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| $d/\mathrm{fm}$ | 33.6 | 25.2 | 20.16 | 16.8 | 12.6 |

sourceAnchors.focus: Coulomb closest approach, nuclear radius and breakdown of Rutherford modelling

questions.changeNotes: Recasts a single-target calculation as a full synthetic reciprocal-energy dataset, uncertainty propagation and explicit model-failure test.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Infer a model parameter from a transformed graph, propagate endpoint uncertainty and distinguish inconsistency from a unique causal conclusion.

verification.method: Reproducible author calculation, dimensional and limiting-case checks
verification.notes: Scattering graph slope = 100.8 MeV fm; Scattering slope uncertainty = 4.8 MeV fm; Target proton number = 35 ; Proton-number uncertainty = 1.666666667 ; Target nuclear radius = 5.170643256 fm; Geometric contact-energy estimate = 19.4946731 MeV; New predicted closest approach = 8.4 fm; New predicted distance uncertainty = 0.4 fm; Physical reasoning and distractor uniqueness: Predicted [8.0,8.8] fm and observed [5.5,6.5] fm do not overlap; that establishes failure of the stated model/error budget without identifying a unique cause.

parts.label: b

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the target proton number and its uncertainty implied by part (b).

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The target nucleon number is $80$ and its radius is modelled by $R=1.20A^{1/3}\,\mathrm{fm}$. Estimate the incident energy at which electrostatic closest approach would equal this radius.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: At $12.0\,\mathrm{MeV}$ a new simulation gives $d=(6.0\pm0.5)\,\mathrm{fm}$. Test its consistency with the electrostatic prediction using your uncertainty in $K$. State one justified limitation of interpreting the discrepancy as proof of a particular nuclear mechanism.

steps.text: Writing $x=1/E$ gives $d=Kx$: a constant gradient K and zero intercept. A nonzero intercept is not predicted by this model.
$Z=K/(2\times1.44)$ and the same constant divisor applies to $\Delta Z$.
$Z=35.0$ with $\Delta Z=4.8/2.88=1.7$. Treating Z as physically integral does not remove the measurement uncertainty; the data are consistent with proton number 35.
$E\approx100.8/5.17=19.5\,\mathrm{MeV}$. This is an estimate of the geometric scale at which the outside-point-charge model ceases to be reliable, not a guaranteed exact onset of a nuclear effect.
The old model predicts $d=100.8/12.0=8.40\,\mathrm{fm}$, with $\Delta d=4.8/12.0=0.40\,\mathrm{fm}$.
The predicted interval $8.0$–$8.8\,\mathrm{fm}$ does not overlap $5.5$–$6.5\,\mathrm{fm}$, so the new result is inconsistent within the stated uncertainties.

The disagreement alone does not establish a unique mechanism: an unmodelled systematic distance/energy bias, finite charge distribution or neglected target response must be checked. Accept another specific, scientifically justified model or calibration limitation; “human error” alone is insufficient.
